newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE-Singapore Inc shifts into high gear in Asia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Singapore Inc shifts into high gear in Asia.

text.p: Becton, Dickinson & Co, a U.S. medical devices and diagnostic products maker, aims to double its sales in Asia by venturing into China and India.
Its launching pad is tiny Singapore -- population three million -- where the government says the economy must regionalise to survive as the powerhouse it has become.
At its Singapore regional headquarters, Becton Dickinson trains managers and workers for its US$40-million factory at the Suzhou Industrial Park near Shanghai.
Becton Dickinson says it plans to invest $100 million in China over the next five years.

"We have a team of people in Singapore most of whom are Chinese speaking," Eugenio Naschold, the company's president for Asia-Pacific told Reuters. "This provided a conduit in building relationships with the Chinese authorities as they arrange the joint venture...and in obtaining permission to produce in China."

Becton Dickinson is among 80 multinational companies (MNCs) and Singapore firms which have joined the Singapore government in pumping more than $2.1 billion into the Suzhou industrial park, a city within a city in Jiangsu province.
Other MNCs investing there include Hitachi Semiconductor, Harris Semiconductor, Siemens, Eli Lilly and RJR Nabisco.

Similar flagship projects, where the government and private sector develop large scale industrial parks, have mushroomed on the Indonesian islands of Batam and Bintan, in the south Indian city of Bangalore, Vietnam's Song Be Province and Wuxi, also in Jiangsu.

A recent survey by the Singapore government's Economic Development Board (EDB), which is pushing the regionalisation strategy, showed the number of investment projects in Asia by Singapore-based companies grew to 443 last year from 381 in 1995.
Total investments surged to $8.06 billion, a sharp 22-percent rise from $6.29 billion in 1995, it said.
Investments in China alone reached $987 million in the first six months of 1996, from $1.86 billion in 1995.

"The overall environment in the region is conducive as nearly all the countries are very competitive in attracting foreign investments," Chua Taik Haim, the EDB's director for international business development said in an interview.
"Singapore companies now are more ready and more aware of the issues, problems and requirements to do a successful regional project...We should be able to maintain the foreign investment momentum."
NEXT TARGET, TO IMPROVE QUALITY
The EDB's target for its next phase of regionalisation is to improve the quality of existing and new projects, not merely to raise the amount of investments or the number of projects.

"I would like to stress that we would like to see the quality of the projects be further improved," Chua said. "We want the projects to grow in substance. It's less a matter to us how many projects we facilitate."
The EDB now seeks projects which can generate more spinoffs and provide more operational linkages with Singapore which can further boost the city state's economy.
To do this, it has put together a more comprehensive support package to help companies, Chua said.

"So when we talk about comprehensive, integrated support, we mean enhancing the capability in the host markets, provide innovation capability, develop the network and knowledge in the country and build partnerships with relevant players."
With the EDB's help, companies were able to tap the large Asian markets and raise their fixed asset investment and value added activities by 10 percent last year, he said.
SMALLER COMPANIES EXPERIENCE DIFFICULTIES
But local small and medium enterprises (SME) trying to respond to the government's regionalisation push have found the road filled with potholes.

"Unlike MNCs such as Seagate which can go into regional countries and negotiate terms for tax incentives and infrastructural support, SMEs like us are weak in those areas," said Tang Yu Kiang, finance manager with Li Xin Group of Companies, a Singapore mould manufacturer.
The firm is looking at investments in China and Thailand "but at this point we have not gone overseas yet," he said.

Li Xin has been seeking a joint venture in Shanghai since September with a Chinese firm linked to the provincial government and another partner to make moulds and metal stamping. But the Chinese side has still not given their reply.

The firm went on a government mission to Thailand and was keen to start business there, but it was discouraged by Bangkok's insistence that the factory be located in southeastern Thailand, not the capital, and found it hard to find the right local partner, Tang said.
"The EDB is just opening up a window, which is better than nothing," he said. "But if we as investors look at the wrong picture, we are in a lot of trouble."
The company still hopes to start a regional venture. If it did not, Li Xin might lose its business of providing materials support to MNC's when they venture abroad, Tang said.
Nor do the big companies always find the EDB-driven projects statisfactory.
Naschold said Becton had talked to the EDB about investing in Bangalore, but decided the land to be allocated to it was too small, and anyway, the industrial park is geared more for electronics.
Becton has instead invested $46 million in Bawal, in north India's Haryana state after dealing directly with the federal government and plans to put in another $54 million in five years.
